Introduction
The Region of Waterloo is growing rapidly. Without sustained new investment, population growth
will outpace ridership growth and move the Region away from its sustainable transportation
targets. Significant transit investment is critical for ridership growth and to help the Region achieve
its strategic priority to grow with care towards one million residents.

Grand River Transit’s Conventional Bus and Train Business Plan is a roadmap to guide transit
investment priorities in Cambridge, Kitchener, and Waterloo to 2035 and beyond. The Plan
demonstrates how the maximum possible transit investment is critical to support the future
needs of the Region.

GRT’s future network includes a comprehensive frequent transit network, more consistent
schedules, strategic expansion, the introduction of highway express services, and an overnight
network. This investment will transform GRT’s network to support a growing population and enable
more Waterloo Region residents and visitors to use transit to get to where they need to go, when
they need to go.

Community engagement
The Plan was developed based on comprehensive technical analysis and multiple phases of
engagement with the public and key contributors:

    •   Phase One (Summer 2024): Introducing the project and identifying the community’s transit
        priorities.

    •   Phase Two (Fall 2024): Collecting public feedback on the preliminary transit investment
        plan priorities.

    •   Phase Three (Winter 2025): Presenting the Plan’s recommendations to contributors and
        decision-makers.

See GRT’s Business Plan Engagement Summary for a detailed summary of GRT’s plan, tactics
and results.

community. Public transit is one of the few dedicated, scalable services the Region is responsible

Yet GRT currently provides less service hours per person than many of Ontario’s largest
municipalities.

Guiding Principles shaped by public engagement
       Simplicity: It is easy, convenient, and intuitive for riders to access and use the GRT
       network. Both new and existing riders understand how to access destinations throughout
       the Region by transit.

       Frequency and speed: Ten-minute daytime service is provided on key routes. GRT trips are
       competitive with car trips. Riders can use GRT to get to where they need to go, when they
       need to go.

       Customer focus: Mature technologies and emerging practices inform services and policies
       that address riders’ needs. GRT strives for continuous improvement with strategic projects.

       Maximizing growth: This Plan includes the maximum possible transit service
       investment, optimizing use of the current and future fleet and staff complement, to enable
       substantial ridership increases over the Plan’s horizon.

Frequent Transit Network (FTN)
The FTN is the core foundation of GRT’s Future
Transit Network and focuses on ridership growth,
network coverage, key corridors and destinations,
and connectivity between the Tri-Cities.

FTN routes include the following:

   •   ION LRT 301
   •   ION Bus / Highway Express 302
   •   Highway Express 303
   •   iXpress 201, 202, 203, 204, 205, and 206.
   •   Local Routes 7, 8, 12, 16, 20, 51, 53, and 61.

The FTN has the potential to save riders more than
20 minutes for transit trips between Conestoga
Station and Ainslie Terminal.

Phasing and Implementation
The future transit network can be implemented over a 10-year period, and requires more buses, a
new Cambridge bus garage, platform access improvements at key ION stations, and system-wide
stop and station expansion. The implementation plan for the future transit network considers these
factors as well as community growth and development plans.

Fare Recommendations
The future transit network features about 60% more service hours compared to today. Accordingly,
the Plan increases fares to match service expansions, inflation, and comparability to peers to
maximize transit service investment.

The following fare recommendations diversify revenues, support service improvements, and
promote affordable access for those who need it most:

   •   Provide free transit for children aged 12 and under, riding with a fare-paying customer, to
       support families and caregivers
   •   Explore opportunities to expand high school transit programs when administrative and
       financial commitments from the boards and/or province can be secured.
   •   Promote reduced public transit costs for seniors through the Ontario Seniors’ Public Transit
       Tax Credit.
   •   Work with agencies and community partners to increase awareness of the existing
       Affordable Transit Program (ATP), and encourage partners to support households in
       completing the application process
   •   Explore greater discounts through a tiered ATP as fare technologies are upgraded.
   •   Maintain existing universal commitment programs (U-Pass)
   •   Use TravelWise to establish commitment-based employer programs through business
       account agreements using GRT’s new mobile payment platform, GRT Pay.

Revenue/Cost Recovery Targets
Revenue/Cost Recovery (R/C) is the ratio of total operating costs compared to revenue recovered
from fares, advertising, etc. It is a key performance metric for GRT and many transit agencies.

The Bus and Train Plan has developed R/C targets by route type. These targets were developed
based on existing GRT route-level R/C performance, literature review, and service and performance
standards from comparable peer agencies.

 Route Type                                       Target R/C Ratio
 Frequent Transit Network
 (includes 301 LRT and 302 ION Bus / Highway      30%-40%
 Express)
 Local Services                                   25%-35%

 303 Highway Express                              20%-30%
 Overnight Network
                                                  5%-15%
 (Midnight – 6am)
 System-wide*                                     35%
* Route-level R/C ratio targets are not directly comparable to the overall System-wide R/C. System-
wide R/C accounts for fixed operating costs, advertising and grant revenues, but route-level R/C
targets do not.

R/C ratios may fluctuate below these targets as routes are modified/introduced throughout the
Plan horizon.

Ridership on new/improved transit services typically takes up to three years to stabilize.

Staffing Requirements
In addition to the Conventional (Bus and Train) Transit Business Plan, GRT recently developed
the MobilityPLUS and Kiwanis Specialized Transit Business Plan and Township Transit
Strategy.

The combined GRT Business Plan features significant transit service increases that require more
GRT staff. Approximately 381 new transit operators, 23 new mechanics, and 8 new fleet
attendants are anticipated to be required to fully realize all elements of the GRT Business Plan.

Additionally, GRT will deliver over 1.6 million service hours annually by 2034, comparable to
several larger transit agencies in the Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area and beyond (e.g., Mississauga
and Winnipeg).

Other large transit agencies feature larger staff complements to support planning, marketing,
fares, customer service, security, HR, and other support functions. Transit systems in Mississauga
and Winnipeg, for example, have roughly 30% more general and administration staff compared
to GRT today.

Next Steps for GRT’s Bus and Train Plan
   •   The Bus and Train investment priorities will guide GRT in preparing future annual service,
       staff, infrastructure, and fleet expansion requests for the Region’s annual Plan and Budget
       process.
   •   The final approved GRT Business Plan will serve as a key input to the Region’s upcoming
       Integrated Mobility Plan (IMP) and area municipalities’ transportation and land use plans.
   •   Transit-supportive policies and programs envisioned in the Region’s IMP and Area
       Municipal plans will be critical for maximizing the ridership potential of the GRT Business
       Plan and shared goals for livable communities.
